text: A real CMDB already has thousands of CIs and no clear service map. In this lesson we'll cover the practical, phased order implementers actually use to apply CSDM — and why starting anywhere other than the business is a common, costly mistake.

CSDM adoption is commonly phased rather than attempted all at once. A sensible phase one identifies the organization's most critical Business Services first — the handful where an outage is expensive or highly visible, judged by revenue impact, customer visibility, and regulatory exposure, not by what's easiest to model. That step can largely happen through conversation with business stakeholders, before touching the CMDB.

The next phase works down one level: identifying the Technical Services that actually deliver each priority Business Service. Order Processing, for example, might depend on an order management application stack and a payment gateway integration. Only in the final phase do you drill into the individual CIs that make up each Technical Service -- the specific servers, databases, and application instances -- and by then, every CI already has a documented reason to matter.

The alternative -- cataloging every CI first and hoping service context gets added later -- is a common, costly mistake. Months can go into inventorying infrastructure with no clear service tie yet, and much of that work gets reorganized or discarded once priorities are finally set, because the people doing the cataloging had no way to know which systems actually mattered most to the business.

Going top-down by priority ties CMDB work directly to business value from day one. The first service modeled correctly is also one of the most important ones, so the payoff shows up early instead of only after the entire estate has been cataloged. Each phase after that one builds on a CMDB that already has real service context, instead of starting over from a pile of ungrouped CIs.
In the lab, you'll apply exactly this chain -- Business Service, Technical Service, and CIs -- to the three-tier application you've been building since Chapter 1.
